abstracts.abstract: We present a novel algebraic framework for dynamic graph connectivity problems that fundamentally rethinks how edge updates are processed. Traditional approaches treat edge insertions and deletions as discrete events requiring complete graph reconstruction. Our framework introduces the concept of *algebraic decomposition* of graph structure, where connectivity queries are answered through evaluating homomorphic mappings over modular arithmetic constructions. We define a new data structure called the *residue connectivity tree* (RCT), which encodes all possible paths between vertices using polynomial-time evaluable functions. The key innovation lies in our observation that the global connectivity structure can be represented as a finite commutative semiring, enabling parallel evaluation of connectivity predicates. We prove that any graph on $n$ vertices admits an RCT representation of size $O(n \log n)$, with query time $O(\log n)$ and update time $O(\log^2 n)$ in the worst case. This represents the first sublinear solution to dynamic connectivity that does not rely on expander-based or routing-based techniques. Our results establish a new connection between algebraic graph theory and online algorithms, opening research directions in parameterized complexity of dynamic problems.

We significantly improve the best-known upper bounds for the online bipartite matching problem under the *rearrangeable network* model, where requests arrive sequentially and must be matched to servers with capacity constraints. The classic result of Goel et al. established a competitive ratio of $O(\log n)$ for this setting. We develop a new analysis technique based on *dual fitting with potential reconstruction* that yields a competitive ratio of $O(\sqrt{\log n})$, improving upon the previous bound by a polynomial factor. Our approach introduces a family of concave potential functions that more accurately capture the structure of feasible matchings in bipartite graphs. We show that the greedy algorithm combined with periodic rebalancing achieves this improved bound, and we prove that no algorithm can achieve $o(\sqrt{\log n})$ competitiveness under standard complexity assumptions. Additionally, we establish a refined lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n}/\log\log n)$ for any deterministic online algorithm, narrowing the gap between upper and lower bounds. Our techniques extend to the generalized assignment problem with unrelated machines, yielding similar improvements in that setting as well.

We present *GraphFlow*, a novel streaming graph processing system designed for continuous analytics on high-velocity data streams. Existing stream processing frameworks treat graph operations as stateless transformations, failing to capture the inherent topological structure of streaming updates. GraphFlow introduces the *incremental view maintenance* paradigm, where graph queries are compiled into incremental computation plans that maintain materialized views over dynamic graph snapshots. Our system architecture comprises three novel components: (1) a *topology-aware partitioning* scheme that co-locates vertices sharing common neighbors to minimize cross-partition communication; (2) a *delta propagation* engine that selectively applies updates to affected subgraph regions; and (3) a *query compiler* that translates declarative graph queries into optimized incremental operators. Experimental evaluation on real-world datasets (Twitter, Reddit, Wikipedia edit streams) demonstrates that GraphFlow achieves 3-8x throughput improvement over state-of-the-art stream processors (Apache Flink, Apache Spark Streaming) for graph analytics workloads including PageRank, connected components, and pattern matching. The system handles up to 10 million edge updates per second on a 16-node cluster while maintaining sub-second latency for analytical queries.

We design and implement *CacheOPT*, a cache-efficient external-memory algorithm for large-scale graph traversal on systems with hierarchical memory. Previous external-memory graph algorithms suffer from poor cache utilization due to irregular access patterns inherent in graph traversal. CacheOPT addresses this through a *hierarchical frontier reorganization* technique that restructures the active vertex set during BFS/DFS traversal to maximize spatial locality. Our key insight is that graph traversal visits vertices in waves, and vertices within the same wave exhibit similar neighborhood structures. By sorting frontier vertices by their predecessor degrees and clustering vertices with similar adjacency patterns, we achieve substantially improved sequential access to adjacency lists. We also introduce a *selective doubling* optimization that maintains small in-memory caches for frequently accessed boundary vertices while streaming less critical data. Implementation on SSDs demonstrates that CacheOPT achieves 2.4-5.1x speedup over the previous state-of-the-art external-memory BFS algorithm (X-Trail) on road networks and web graphs. For billion-edge graphs, CacheOPT reduces I/O operations by 68% and achieves complete traversal within 4 hours on commodity hardware, compared to 15+ hours for competitors.
